title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education Footfalls Echo in the Memory
author: James, David A.
summary: James argues that learning poetry by heart -- once standard in English education -- is a profound pedagogical gift largely denied to students today. Drawing on his own experience memorising Shakespeare and Milton at fifteen, he shows that memorised verse becomes inseparable from a person's identity decades later. His Year 9 classroom protocol begins with analytical study (written responses on difficulty, ambiguity, form, and theme), then memorisation, then unannounced retrieval practice in later lessons to interrupt the forgetting curve. Some students memorised Shelley's Ozymandias word-perfect in eighteen minutes -- surprising themselves by what their capacity actually was when the expectation was real. The exercise generated dinner-table conversations in which parents recited poems from their own schooling, demonstrating how memorised verse travels across generations. James contends that AI cannot help with this task, that mobile phones have eroded the expectation that it is possible, and that teachers should restore the demanding assumption that students can and should carry great writing inside them.
points: - Poetry learned by heart becomes so embedded in identity that forty years later the author cannot disentangle the memorised lines from his own worldview -- the poems are 'me,' not merely something I know. - The analytical study before memorisation is load-bearing: pupils must write about difficulty, ambiguity, form, and theme before committing lines to memory, giving the words conceptual hooks to anchor to. - Retrieval practice is deliberately built into the protocol -- calling on students without notice in later lessons interrupts the forgetting curve and pushes material toward long-term memory. - Students consistently underestimate their mnemonic capacity when the expectation is real: some memorised Ozymandias perfectly in eighteen minutes, far faster than they anticipated. - The ripple effect beyond school is undervalued: memorised poems prompted family conversations where parents recited their own school-era poems, creating cross-generational encounters with literature that no worksheet produces.
quotes: Sometimes the past comes back to you, fully formed and in iambic pentameter. Ever since I learned Portia's speech from Act 4, Scene 1 of The Merchant of Venice, it resurfaces when I see an abuse of power or a misunderstanding of justice. I learned it for homework when I was fifteen; forty years later, it is still with me.

When I think of the sheer volume of lines we had to learn for these examinations, it astonishes me that we were not just able to do so, but that we were so unquestioning in our acceptance that this was not just advisable but also possible. But these were in the days before mobile phones.

I must have resented having to learn so many lines, but that bitterness has long gone, and they are now such a part of me that I cannot disentangle them from my own view of myself. They are me and, as I say, are more perfectly constructed than the sub-linguistic memories dredged up from some insalubrious corner of my past.
More than that, though, I feel they are a finer part of me, a clear gift from a writer, via a teacher, to my childhood self, and one which I still try to pass on.

Some of the pupils talked about how the task had opened up conversations with parents and other relatives about the poems they had learned when they were in school: Shelley was there, Shakespeare too, and other names mentioned.

But the real test, I said to them, will be in the weeks to come when I ask, without notice, for them to recite the poems they've learned; that strain of recall will successfully interrupt the forgetting curve and will, hopefully, embed the words, and their meaning, still further.

I gave them The Road Not Taken by Robert Frost and asked them to annotate it. We then went through each stanza and explored why it is not simply about a path not taken. The written work I have asked for is a little difficult, but sometimes pupils will surprise you if you set them something probably suited for older students.
